title: Strength Has a Kidney Context
subtitle: Chronic kidney disease does not automatically rule out resistance training. It does make the right plan personal—shaped by health, treatment, access and the person’s own goals.
imageAlt: Two friends talk with an exercise professional beside a chair and resistance bands in a bright community gym.
imageConcept: A warm, everyday scene in a small community gym: two adult friends sit beside one another while an exercise professional listens and points to a resistance band and chair. The focus is on shared planning and choice, not medical equipment or dramatic exertion.
body: Kidney disease changes the plan, not the value of strength

A diagnosis of chronic kidney disease (CKD) can make exercise feel like territory that belongs to someone else: the clinic, the specialist, the person who is already fit. But CKD is not, by itself, a universal instruction to avoid strength activity. The more useful question is what kind of movement fits this person’s health, treatment and priorities—and what support would make it workable.

That distinction matters because “exercise” can mean many things: everyday activity, a planned walk, or structured training with resistance. A 2025 practical guide from the Global Renal Exercise Network emphasizes tailoring activity to health information, goals, preferences and possible contraindications rather than prescribing one template for everyone [1]. The starting point can be modest and collaborative. Someone may want to feel steadier carrying groceries; someone else may want to return to a familiar class. Neither goal needs to be translated into a generic fitness ideal before it can be discussed.
The label CKD does not tell the whole story

CKD covers a range of health situations. The stage of disease is one part of the picture; coexisting conditions, physical capacity, treatment and recent changes matter too. Two people with the same diagnosis may have different reasons for choosing a movement, adapting it or waiting for guidance. A plan that ignores those differences risks being either unnecessarily restrictive or too confident.

A UK clinical practice guideline discusses exercise across non-dialysis CKD, haemodialysis and kidney-transplant contexts, and recommends strength-oriented activity for people with non-dialysis CKD. It also stresses that exercise programmes should be supervised and led by suitably qualified people [2]. That is useful evidence for keeping strength in the conversation, not a universal prescription: the guideline reflects a UK context, and an individual’s care team can help interpret what applies. The practical point is to describe the person in front of you—not reduce them to a stage, a treatment label or an assumption about what they can do.
Separate everyday movement from a training programme

A practical first step is to name what you mean by “getting stronger.” It might mean more confidence standing from a chair, lifting a light object, gardening, or following a structured resistance programme. These are not interchangeable plans. Being clear about the intended activity helps a clinician or qualified exercise professional consider its demands and how it might fit alongside current care.

The Global Renal Exercise Network guide treats general physical activity and structured exercise as distinct parts of the discussion [1]. That distinction can make a conversation more useful: instead of asking only, “Can I exercise?”, bring a real example. What movement are you considering? How often would it happen? What equipment or position does it involve? What would you like it to help you do? If a formal programme is not a fit right now, that does not make all movement off limits; it means the next step is to clarify which options are appropriate with the people who know your health circumstances.

A short, prepared conversation can replace vague reassurance with a plan that has boundaries. Before an appointment, write down the activity you have in mind, the reason it matters to you, and any practical constraints: fatigue, pain, balance, transport, cost or access to equipment. Ask whether there are health considerations that should shape the activity, whether a referral to a qualified exercise professional is appropriate, and what changes would mean you should pause and check in.

If you already see a physiotherapist or exercise professional, ask how they will coordinate with your kidney-care team. The clinical guide recommends considering health information and potential contraindications when planning activity [1]; the UK guideline’s emphasis on qualified supervision supports asking who is prepared to lead the programme [2]. This is not a test of whether you have earned permission to move. It is a way to put the relevant people and information around the decision, so the plan reflects your goals without pretending that every health detail is interchangeable.
Dialysis and access call for extra attention

For people receiving dialysis, timing and access are part of the training conversation. The practical guide flags treatment stability and avoiding physical damage to a catheter, fistula or transplant site as considerations [1]. That is a reason to ask for advice specific to the access and the activity—not to assume that every movement is safe, or that all strength work is automatically forbidden.

The published advice for people receiving dialysis is not perfectly uniform. A 2022 scoping review found variation in recommendations on timing, intensity, progression and safety; it also found limited detail about access precautions in the guidance it reviewed [3]. That uncertainty argues against borrowing a routine from a friend, a video or a general gym plan and assuming it transfers. Ask the dialysis team which movements, positions, loading or timing need to be modified, and who should be consulted if access-related questions arise. Keep the answer with the person’s actual treatment arrangements, and revisit it if those arrangements or health circumstances change.
Turn advice into a usable first plan

Once the relevant guidance is clear, make it concrete enough to follow. Start by agreeing on the setting and the person responsible for supervision, if supervision is recommended. Choose an activity that matches the person’s stated goal and the equipment they can reliably access. Confirm any limits or modifications with the clinician or qualified professional before beginning; do not infer them from a diagnosis or from someone else’s programme.

Then settle the practical details: where the activity will happen, how it fits around treatment and other commitments, and how the person will record what they tried. For an early session, the useful question is not whether it looked impressive. It is whether the agreed activity was manageable in that setting and whether anything needs to be discussed before repeating it. The dialysis review’s finding that published guidance varies makes this kind of individual planning especially important [3]. Keep the plan adjustable rather than treating the first version as a contract.
Progress by checking in, not by guessing

A strength plan should have a way to change. At agreed intervals, review what the person has been doing, how it fits into daily life and whether their goals have shifted. Bring new symptoms, treatment changes, access concerns or uncertainty back to the care team rather than trying to diagnose the cause or push through a problem. Ask in advance what signs mean to stop and seek advice, so that decision is not improvised during a session.

Progress does not have to mean adding more resistance or chasing a performance target. It can mean finding a schedule that is easier to sustain, adapting a movement, or discovering that a different form of support is needed. The 2025 guide’s emphasis on preferences and health context is a reminder that adherence is not simply willpower; a plan has to fit the person who will live with it [1]. If the current approach is not working, treat that as information for a revised conversation—not evidence that the person has failed.

CKD can make exercise planning more complex, particularly when dialysis, cardiovascular concerns, other conditions or a transplant are part of the picture. Complexity is not the same as a blanket no. Clinical guidance supports considering strength-oriented activity in relevant CKD contexts while also calling for attention to supervision, individual circumstances and treatment-specific precautions [1][2]. For dialysis, the research review shows why precise, shared guidance matters: published recommendations do not answer every practical question in the same way [3].

The most useful plan is therefore neither an unqualified promise nor an automatic prohibition. It is a specific conversation about the movement someone wants to do, the health details that shape it, the professional support available and the way the plan will be reviewed. That leaves room for caution without letting caution erase the person’s goals. Strength remains a worthwhile subject to raise—with the person at the centre of the decision.
